results.summary: This design is a read-only memory that stores ASCII encodings of LaTeX code for a few dozen Laplace transforms, generated by a Python script from the LaTeX source. The user selects a transform index on the lower six input pins, toggles reset, then asserts the character output enable to clock out the transform characters one at a time. The left-hand side output shows the transformed function F(s) and the right-hand side output shows the original function f(t), padded with spaces when lengths differ. External switches or jumpers are needed to set the input address and enable signals, and LEDs on the outputs help observe the characters; the documentation is detailed and includes verification via the same Python script.

This is a simple TTL pulse generator that produces one of sixteen pre-programmed pulse sequences selected by a 4-bit input. The selected sequence appears on a single TTL output pin, and the design is intended to be tested by setting the sequence select pins and observing the output. No external hardware is required beyond the chip itself, though the documentation does not describe the sequences or their timing. The documentation is very thin, providing only the basic function and pin usage.

This design generates a VGA test pattern resembling NTSC color bars, with optional station ID display, scrolling ID, and scrolling bars. It is configured through input pins for showing the ID, using a custom ID, scrolling the ID, and scrolling the bars, and it outputs RGB and sync signals on the Tiny VGA pinout. A TinyVGA PMOD is required to connect to a VGA monitor, and the colors are explicitly not accurate to real NTSC color bars. Silicon test reports indicate it works, though one tester noted the clock must be manually set to 25 MHz in the commander app.

This design implements hardware logic to convert Unicode code points between UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32 encodings. It detects and signals errors such as overlong encodings, out-of-range code points, and invalid byte sequences, with an option to disable range checking for the original UTF-8 specification. The design is tested via a Python test suite covering a comprehensive set of cases, and it is intended for use in any device that processes Unicode text. The documentation is thorough, describing the error signals and test methodology.

This design displays a large selection of pride flags on a VGA monitor, with controls to show the first flag, move to the next or previous flag, or select a flag by index. It uses the Tiny VGA pinout and requires a TinyVGA PMOD to connect to a monitor. The design is extensible by adding new flag modules and updating the index, as described in the documentation. No silicon test reports are provided, but the documentation is clear about usage and configuration.

This is a Verilog replica of the AY-3-8913 programmable sound generator, providing three square-wave tone channels, a white noise generator, and an envelope generator with ten shapes. It is programmed through a multiplexed data/address bus with bus control pins, and it outputs digital 8-bit audio as well as PWM signals for each channel and a master audio output. External hardware such as a DAC, RC filter, amplifier, and speaker are needed to hear the audio, and the design includes a configurable clock divider to match different clock frequencies. The project is notable for its thorough test suite and goal of hardware preservation, fitting on a single Tiny Tapeout tile.

This design is a Verilog replica of the SN76489 programmable sound generator, featuring three square-wave tone channels, a noise generator with white and periodic modes, and 16 levels of attenuation per channel. It is controlled via an 8-bit data bus with a write-enable pin, and it provides digital 8-bit audio output plus PWM outputs for each channel and a master audio output. External hardware such as a DAC, RC filter, amplifier, and speaker are required to produce sound, and the design includes a configurable clock divider. The project emphasizes hardware preservation and includes a comprehensive test suite, fitting on a single tile.

This design computes the Collatz sequence for a large integer input, returning the orbit length and an indicator of the maximum value reached. The input number is uploaded byte-by-byte into a 144-bit register via an address bus, and the computation is started with a pin; the busy indicator is polled until completion, after which the results are read back in 16-bit chunks. The design is intended for brute-force searching of path records, and the documentation explains the state machine and I/O protocol in detail. No external hardware is required beyond the chip itself.

This is a demoscene demo for Tiny Tapeout that generates both VGA video and audio, using the Tiny VGA and audio PMODs. It is written in Silice and can be simulated on an ECPIX5 with a VGA PMOD and an I2S audio PMOD, or the audio can run on an ULX3S using its DAC. The documentation is minimal, consisting mainly of a rhetorical question and a note that it works as expected when tested with the PMODs. The design is notable for being part of a demoscene competition and for combining video and audio in a small area.

This is a demoscene demo for Tiny Tapeout that produces a VGA video effect and audio, using the Tiny VGA and audio PMODs. It is written in Silice and is intended to be run by plugging in the PMODs, with a silicon test report confirming it works as expected with the Tiny VGA PMOD. The documentation is extremely sparse, providing only a one-line description and a rhetorical question, so little is known about the specific visual or audio content. The design is notable for being part of a demoscene competition and for fitting on a single tile.
